names.meaning: 'He (God) enlightens' or 'he will awaken'

roles: Father who sought healing for his daughter
occupations: Ruler of a synagogue (archisynagōgos), a lay leader who arranged the services

events.title: Begs Jesus to come to his dying daughter
events.summary: When Jesus lands on the Galilean shore, Jairus falls at his feet and pleads for his twelve-year-old daughter, his only daughter in Luke's telling, who is near death.

events.title: Delay on the road
events.summary: On the way, Jesus stops to speak with a woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years and touched his cloak. During the delay, word comes that the girl has died.

events.title: His daughter raised
events.summary: Jesus tells Jairus, 'Do not fear, only believe.' Taking only Peter, James and John and the parents, he takes the girl's hand and says 'Talitha cumi' (Aramaic for 'little girl, arise'). She gets up and walks, and Jesus tells them to give her something to eat.

summary: Jairus was a leader of a local synagogue in Galilee who came to Jesus when his twelve-year-old daughter was dying. Mark and Luke name him; Matthew tells a shorter version and calls him simply 'a ruler'. His story is wrapped around the healing of a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years, so the two stories are meant to be read together: both involve 'twelve years', both involve faith, and both involve a woman who is ritually unclean (by illness or death) being restored by Jesus' touch. The setting is by the Sea of Galilee, probably at or near Capernaum, though the text does not say so directly.
textSays: Mark 5:22 and Luke 8:41 name him Jairus and call him a ruler of the synagogue. Luke 8:42 says the girl was his only daughter, about twelve years old. Matthew 9:18 says the ruler came saying his daughter had just died, a compressed form of the story. Mark 5:41 preserves Jesus' Aramaic words.

interpretations.view: The story shows that a respected religious official and an outcast woman come to Jesus on the same terms: need and trust.
Many scholars see Mark's 'sandwich' technique here, where one story is placed inside another so each explains the other.

voice: A dignified man stripped of his dignity by fear for his child; speaks urgently, then in hushed wonder.

names.meaning: 'Son of Timaeus' (Timaeus may mean 'honoured')

events.title: Cries out to the Son of David and receives sight
events.summary: Sitting by the road outside Jericho, he shouts 'Son of David, have mercy on me' and refuses to be silenced. Jesus calls him, he throws off his cloak, asks to see again, is healed, and follows Jesus on the road toward Jerusalem.

summary: Bartimaeus was a blind beggar at Jericho healed by Jesus on his last journey to Jerusalem. Mark alone names him. Luke tells of one unnamed blind man (Luke 18:35-43), and Matthew of two (Matt 20:29-34). He is the only person Jesus heals in Mark who is said to follow him 'on the road' afterwards.
textSays: Mark 10:46 says he was the son of Timaeus and sat by the roadside begging. He calls Jesus 'Son of David', a royal title for the Messiah (Mark 10:47). Jesus says his faith has made him well (Mark 10:52).

interpretations.view: Matthew's two men and Mark's one may be the same event: Mark and Luke focus on the better-known man, perhaps because Bartimaeus was later known to the church.
Many scholars think Matthew doubled the figure (as he also does with the Gadarene demoniacs) and that the name in Mark points to an eyewitness known to Mark's first readers.

voice: Loud, stubborn and unembarrassed; he will not let a chance pass him by.

names.meaning: Simon (from Hebrew Shimon, 'he has heard'); Cyrene was a city in North Africa (modern Libya)

events.title: Forced to carry the cross
events.summary: Coming in from the countryside, he is pressed into service by the Roman soldiers to carry Jesus' cross to the place of execution.

summary: Simon was a man from Cyrene, a North African city with a large Jewish community, who was in Jerusalem at Passover. Roman soldiers forced him to carry Jesus' cross. Mark adds that he was the father of Alexander and Rufus, which suggests Mark's readers knew those sons.
textSays: Mark 15:21 calls him 'the father of Alexander and Rufus' and says he was coming in from the country. Matthew 27:32 and Luke 23:26 also tell the event; Luke says he carried it 'behind Jesus'.

interpretations.view: Some suggest the Rufus greeted in Romans 16:13 is his son, and some link him to 'Simeon called Niger' in Acts 13:1. Both are possible but unproven (speculative).
Luke's phrase 'behind Jesus' echoes Jesus' call to take up the cross and follow (Luke 9:23), so Simon becomes a picture of discipleship.

traditions.text: Some Gnostic writers taught that Simon was crucified in Jesus' place; the early church rejected this, and Irenaeus reports it as the teaching of Basilides.

voice: A plain-spoken traveller, startled at being dragged into a stranger's execution, later thoughtful about what he saw.

names.meaning: 'Son of the father' (or son of a man named Abba)
aliases: Jesus Barabbas (in some manuscripts of Matthew)

events.title: Released at the crowd's demand
events.summary: Pilate offers to release a prisoner for the Passover. The crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, asks for Barabbas, and Jesus is handed over to be crucified.

summary: Barabbas was a prisoner held for taking part in a rebellion in Jerusalem in which a murder was committed. At Jesus' trial the crowd asked Pilate to free him instead of Jesus. All four Gospels tell the scene. Some early manuscripts of Matthew call him 'Jesus Barabbas', which would make the crowd's choice between two men named Jesus.
textSays: Mark 15:7 says he was in prison with rebels who had committed murder in the uprising. Luke 23:19 says he was thrown into prison for insurrection and murder. John 18:40 calls him a lēstēs, a word for a bandit often used of armed rebels. Matthew 27:16 calls him a notorious prisoner.

interpretations.view: Many Christians see Barabbas as a picture of substitution: the guilty man goes free while the innocent one dies.

No source outside the Gospels mentions a custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover. Some historians doubt the custom; others point to known cases of Roman governors granting amnesties and argue a local practice is plausible.

voice: Hard and defiant, a man of the street fight, baffled at his sudden freedom.

names.meaning: 'King' or 'counsellor'

occupations: Household servant of the high priest

events.title: Ear cut off and healed at the arrest
events.summary: When the crowd comes to arrest Jesus, Peter draws a sword and cuts off Malchus's right ear. Jesus tells Peter to put the sword away, and in Luke he touches the ear and heals it.

summary: Malchus was a servant of the high priest who came with the group that arrested Jesus in the garden. All four Gospels report that a disciple cut off a servant's ear, but only John names both the servant (Malchus) and the swordsman (Peter). Only Luke says Jesus healed the ear: the last healing miracle before the cross.
textSays: John 18:10 gives his name and says it was the right ear. John 18:26 mentions a relative of Malchus who recognized Peter in the courtyard. Luke 22:51 says Jesus touched the ear and healed him. Matthew 26:51-52 and Mark 14:47 do not name him.

interpretations.view: The scene is often used to teach that Jesus' kingdom is not advanced by violence and that he showed mercy even to those arresting him.
Many scholars think John's naming of Malchus, and of a relative of his, shows contact with someone who knew the high priest's household (compare John 18:15-16).

voice: A servant doing his master's errand who never expected to be touched by the man he came to seize; shaken and quiet.

names.meaning: 'The LORD has been gracious'

roles: Disciple and financial supporter of Jesus

events.title: Travels with Jesus and supports the mission
events.summary: Healed by Jesus of 'evil spirits and infirmities', she joins the women who travel with him and the Twelve and provide for them out of their own means.

events.title: Goes to the tomb and reports to the apostles
events.summary: She is among the women who watch the burial, prepare spices, find the tomb empty, hear the angels, and tell the apostles, who at first do not believe them.

summary: Joanna was a Galilean woman whom Jesus had healed, and the wife of Chuza, the steward (household manager) of Herod Antipas. That means she came from the edge of the royal court, the same court that executed John the Baptist. She travelled with Jesus, helped pay for the mission, and was one of the women who found the tomb empty and told the apostles. She appears only in Luke.
textSays: Luke 8:3 calls her 'the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward' and says she and others provided for Jesus' group from their possessions. Luke 24:10 lists her with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James as those who told the apostles about the empty tomb.

interpretations.view: Luke may have known Herod's court partly through her (compare Luke 23:8-12 and Manaen in Acts 13:1); this is a suggestion, not something the text says.
Richard Bauckham has argued she is the same person as Junia in Romans 16:7, using a Latin name; most scholars treat this as possible but unproven (speculative).

voice: Well-spoken and composed, with the manners of a court household, but warm and direct about what Jesus did for her.

names.meaning: 'Lily'

roles: Disciple and financial supporter of Jesus

events.title: Travels with Jesus and the Twelve
events.summary: Named among the women healed by Jesus who travel with him and support the group from their own means.

summary: Susanna is named once, in Luke 8:3, among the women who travelled with Jesus and paid for the mission out of their own money. Nothing else is known about her. Her mention shows that Jesus' traveling company included several women of some means, not only the Twelve.
textSays: Luke 8:2-3 lists her after Mary Magdalene and Joanna, as one of 'many others' who provided for them.
voice: Quiet and practical, the sort who keeps the group fed and says little about it.

names.meaning: 'Peace'
aliases: Possibly the mother of the sons of Zebedee

roles: Witness of the crucifixion and empty tomb

events.title: Watches the crucifixion
events.summary: She is among the women from Galilee who had followed and served Jesus and who watch his death from a distance.

events.title: Brings spices to the tomb
events.summary: Early on the first day of the week she goes with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James to anoint the body, and finds the stone rolled away.

summary: Salome was a Galilean woman who followed Jesus, watched his crucifixion, and went to the tomb on Easter morning. Mark is the only Gospel that names her. She is not the same person as Salome the daughter of Herodias, who is never named in the Bible.
textSays: Mark 15:40 lists her with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses. Mark 16:1 has her buy spices to anoint Jesus' body.

interpretations.view: Matthew's parallel list (Matt 27:56) has 'the mother of the sons of Zebedee' where Mark has Salome, so many readers conclude she was the mother of James and John.
Some also identify her with 'his mother's sister' in John 19:25, which would make her Jesus' aunt and James and John his cousins. Others read John 19:25 differently, and the link remains uncertain.

voice: Steady and loyal, with a mother's bluntness; she stays when others run.

names.meaning: Mary (from Hebrew Miryam); 'of Clopas' can mean wife, or less likely daughter, of Clopas
aliases: Possibly Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses

events.title: Stands by the cross
events.summary: John names her among the women standing near the cross with Jesus' mother and Mary Magdalene.

summary: Mary the wife of Clopas is named only in John 19:25, standing by the cross. Who she was beyond that is debated. Many identify her with 'Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses' in Mark and with 'the other Mary' in Matthew, who also went to the tomb. If so, she was one of the first witnesses of the resurrection.
textSays: John 19:25 lists 'his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene'. The Greek can be read as three women (with Mary of Clopas being the mother's sister) or four women.

interpretations.tradition: Identification with Mary mother of James and Joses (debated)
interpretations.view: The lists of women at the cross (Mark 15:40; Matt 27:56) include a Mary who is mother of James the younger and Joses; many scholars take her to be the same as Mary of Clopas. Others think these are different women.

If John lists three women, she is called the 'sister' of Jesus' mother. Since two sisters are unlikely to share the name Mary, many take 'sister' loosely as sister-in-law, which fits the report that Clopas was Joseph's brother.

traditions.text: Hegesippus, a second-century Jewish Christian writer, says Clopas was the brother of Joseph and that his son Symeon became leader of the Jerusalem church after James.

voice: A family woman, steady and grieving, who speaks of Jesus almost as kin.

names.original: Greek Kleopas, probably short for Kleopatros
names.meaning: 'Of a renowned father' (Greek)

roles: Disciple who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus

events.title: The walk to Emmaus
events.summary: On Easter Sunday he and a companion walk to Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. A stranger joins them and explains from the Scriptures why the Messiah had to suffer. At supper he breaks bread, they recognize Jesus, and he vanishes. They hurry back to Jerusalem to tell the eleven.

journey.note: Leaves Jerusalem downcast on the first day of the week.
Recognizes the risen Jesus in the breaking of bread.
Returns the same hour to report to the eleven.

summary: Cleopas was one of two disciples who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus without recognizing him. His companion is not named. He is a follower outside the Twelve, and his story is one of the most detailed resurrection appearances in the Gospels.
textSays: Luke 24:18 names him. Luke 24:21 records his disappointment: 'we had hoped he was the one to redeem Israel'. Luke 24:32 records the two saying their hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures.

interpretations.view: Some identify him with Clopas, the husband of one of the Marys at the cross (John 19:25); if so, his unnamed companion may have been his wife. Others note that Kleopas (a Greek name) and Klōpas (probably Semitic) are spelled differently and may be different men.
The Emmaus story is often read as a model for Christian worship: Scripture opened, then bread broken, and Jesus known in both.

voice: Honest about his disappointment, quick to talk, and then bursting with excitement.

names.primary: The Samaritan woman at the well
names.meaning: The text does not give her name

roles: Witness to her town about Jesus

events.title: Conversation at Jacob's well
events.summary: At noon Jesus, tired, asks her for a drink. She is surprised, since Jews and Samaritans avoided sharing vessels. He speaks of 'living water', reveals that she has had five husbands and lives with a man who is not her husband, and discusses where God should be worshipped. He then tells her plainly that he is the Messiah.

events.title: Brings her town to Jesus
events.summary: She leaves her water jar and tells the townspeople, 'Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did.' Many believe because of her word, and more after hearing Jesus for two days.

summary:
This unnamed Samaritan woman had the longest recorded one-to-one conversation with Jesus in the Gospels. Samaritans lived between Judea and Galilee and worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem; Jews and Samaritans were long-standing rivals. Jesus crossed that line, and the line between men and women in public, to speak with her. She became the first person in John's Gospel to tell a whole town about him.

Readers often assume she was an immoral outcast because she came at noon and had five husbands. The text does not say why she had five husbands; she may have been widowed or divorced (only men could initiate divorce), and many scholars now caution against reading her mainly as a 'sinful woman'.
textSays: John 4:9 says Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. John 4:18 says she has had five husbands and the man she now has is not her husband. John 4:26 has Jesus say 'I who speak to you am he.' John 4:39 says many Samaritans believed because of her testimony.

interpretations.view: Many preachers present her as a woman with a scandalous past whom Jesus gently exposes and restores.
Others stress that the text never calls her sinful, and that she acts like a theological conversation partner and an evangelist, much like the disciples who bring others to Jesus in John 1.
She is honoured as a saint and 'equal to the apostles' for her preaching.

traditions.text: Orthodox tradition names her Photini (or Photina, 'the enlightened one') and says she preached widely and was martyred under the emperor Nero. The text itself gives no name.
traditions.source: Orthodox Synaxarion; commemorated on the Sunday of the Samaritan Woman, the fifth Sunday after Pascha

voice: Sharp, quick-witted and unafraid to argue theology with a stranger; then eager and breathless as she runs to tell others.

names.meaning: 'He has heard' (from Hebrew Shimon)

roles: Pharisee who hosted Jesus for a meal
occupations: Pharisee (member of a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law)

events.title: A sinful woman anoints Jesus at his table
events.summary: While Jesus eats at Simon's house, a woman known as a sinner weeps on his feet, wipes them with her hair, and anoints them. Simon privately doubts Jesus is a prophet. Jesus tells him a parable of two debtors and points out that Simon gave him no water, kiss or oil, while she has shown great love because she has been forgiven much.

summary: Simon was a Pharisee in Galilee who invited Jesus to dinner. When a woman with a bad reputation came in and anointed Jesus' feet, Simon judged both her and Jesus, and Jesus answered with a short parable about forgiveness. The story is told only in Luke and leaves Simon's response open.
textSays: Luke 7:36 says a Pharisee invited Jesus; Luke 7:40 gives his name as Simon. Luke 7:39 records his inner thought that a prophet would know what sort of woman she was. Luke 7:44-46 lists the courtesies he did not offer.

interpretations.view: Mark, Matthew and John tell of an anointing at Bethany in Jesus' last week, Mark and Matthew at the house of 'Simon the leper'. Some think Luke's story is a different, earlier event; others think the Gospels preserve varied forms of one event. Most scholars treat Luke's account as a separate event or a separate tradition.
Simon stands for the respectable person who sees others' sins more readily than his own need of forgiveness.

voice: Polite, reserved and quietly judgmental, a careful host who keeps a guest at arm's length.

names.meaning: 'Simon the leper', probably a man once ill with a skin disease, perhaps healed

events.title: Jesus anointed in his house
events.summary: Two days before Passover, while Jesus is at table in Simon's house, a woman pours very costly ointment on his head. Some complain about the waste; Jesus says she has anointed his body for burial and will be remembered wherever the gospel is preached.

summary: Simon the leper lived at Bethany near Jerusalem and hosted a meal for Jesus in the last week before his death. He is known only by this nickname. Since a person with an active skin disease would have lived apart from others, many think he had been healed, possibly by Jesus, though the text does not say so.
textSays: Mark 14:3 and Matthew 26:6 place the anointing 'in the house of Simon the leper' at Bethany. John 12:1-8 tells of a dinner at Bethany where Martha served, Lazarus reclined, and Mary anointed Jesus' feet, but does not name the host.

interpretations.view: Many think John's dinner at Bethany is the same event, held at Simon's house. Some later writers guessed Simon was a relative of Martha, Mary and Lazarus, or even their father; this is speculation.
A minority identify him with Simon the Pharisee of Luke 7, treating the anointings as one event; most scholars keep them apart.

voice: Grateful and hospitable, a man who knows what it is to be shut out and now opens his door.

names.meaning: Feminine form of Herod

roles: Instigator of John the Baptist's execution

events.title: Leaves her husband to marry Antipas
events.summary: She divorces her first husband, Herod Antipas's half-brother, and marries Antipas. John the Baptist publicly condemns the marriage as against the Law (Lev 18:16).

events.title: Demands the head of John the Baptist
events.summary: She holds a grudge against John. At Herod's birthday banquet her daughter pleases Herod with a dance and, prompted by Herodias, asks for John's head on a platter.

events.title: Follows Antipas into exile
events.summary: According to Josephus, when the emperor Caligula banished Antipas to Gaul, he offered to spare Herodias, but she chose to go into exile with her husband.

summary: Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great who married two of her uncles in turn. Her second marriage, to Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, was publicly condemned by John the Baptist, since she had left Antipas's brother while he was still alive. The Gospels present her as the driving force behind John's beheading. The Jewish historian Josephus adds that she later went with Antipas into exile in Gaul in AD 39.
textSays: Mark 6:17-18 says Herod married Herodias, 'his brother Philip's wife', and John said it was not lawful. Mark 6:19 says she nursed a grudge and wanted to kill John but could not, until the banquet. Luke 3:19 says John rebuked Herod about Herodias.
context: Josephus (*Antiquities* 18.5.4) says she was the daughter of Aristobulus, a son of Herod the Great, and that her first husband was a son of Herod the Great called simply Herod. Mark calls this first husband Philip. Some think he had a double name; others think Mark confused him with Philip the tetrarch, who in fact married Herodias's daughter (debated). Josephus (*Antiquities* 18.7.1-2) tells of her ambition pushing Antipas to seek the title of king, which led to his downfall.

interpretations.view: She is often compared to Jezebel, the queen who hunted the prophet Elijah (1 Kgs 19:2), with John playing the role of a new Elijah.
Josephus gives a political reason for John's death (Herod feared an uprising), while the Gospels give a personal one; many historians think both factors could be true together.

voice: Proud, calculating and fiercely protective of her position; speaks with cold precision.

names.meaning: 'Peace'; the Gospels do not give her name, which comes from Josephus

occupations: Royal princess; later wife of Philip the tetrarch and then of Aristobulus of Chalcis

events.title: Dances at Herod's birthday and asks for John's head
events.summary: Her dance pleases Herod Antipas, who rashly promises her anything. After asking her mother what to request, she asks for John the Baptist's head on a platter, and receives it.

summary: The Gospels call her only 'the daughter of Herodias' and describe her as a young girl. The Jewish historian Josephus names Herodias's daughter as Salome and says she later married her great-uncle Philip the tetrarch, and after his death her cousin Aristobulus. She is a different person from Salome the follower of Jesus.
textSays: Mark 6:22 says the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased Herod and his guests; Mark 6:24 says she went out and asked her mother what to request. Mark 6:22 and 6:28 call her korasion, 'girl'. Some manuscripts of Mark 6:22 read 'his daughter Herodias', which creates a textual puzzle.
context: Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.5.4, gives her name and marriages. Coins from her later marriage to Aristobulus show her portrait. The famous 'Dance of the Seven Veils' comes from Oscar Wilde's 1891 play, not the Bible.

interpretations.view: The text puts the blame mainly on Herodias, with the girl acting as her mother's instrument and Herod as the weak ruler who fears losing face.
Medieval and modern art often turned her into a seductive figure; the Gospels say nothing about seduction and call her a girl.

voice: Young, eager to please, turning to her mother for the answer.

names.meaning: 'Lover of horses'
aliases: Philip, tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis

alternatives.label: If Herod the Great died in 1 BC

roles: Tetrarch (ruler of a quarter) of the lands north-east of Galilee

events.title: Ruler in the fifteenth year of Tiberius
events.summary: Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry partly by naming Philip as tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis.

events.title: Builder of Caesarea Philippi
events.summary: He rebuilt the town of Paneas at the springs of the Jordan and renamed it Caesarea in honour of the emperor; it became known as Caesarea Philippi, where Peter later confessed Jesus as the Messiah.

summary: Philip was a son of Herod the Great who ruled the mostly non-Jewish lands north-east of the Sea of Galilee from 4 BC until his death in AD 34. Josephus remembers him as a mild and fair ruler. He rebuilt Paneas as Caesarea Philippi and enlarged Bethsaida, renaming it Julias. He married Salome, the daughter of Herodias.
textSays: Luke 3:1 names him as tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis. The Gospels mention the city he named, Caesarea Philippi (Matt 16:13).
context: Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.4.6, records his death in the twentieth year of Tiberius after ruling 37 years. Mark 6:17 calls Herodias's first husband 'Philip'; most historians think this was a different son of Herod (called Herod by Josephus), not the tetrarch, though some think Mark refers to the tetrarch (debated).
voice: Measured and administrative, more interested in building towns and minting coins than in religious quarrels.

names.meaning: 'Ruler of the people'

alternatives.label: If Herod the Great died in 1 BC

roles: Ethnarch (ruler of a people) of Judea, Samaria and Idumea

events.title: Joseph avoids Judea because of him
events.summary: After Herod the Great dies, Joseph hears that Archelaus is ruling Judea in his father's place and is afraid to go there; warned in a dream, he settles the family in Nazareth in Galilee.

events.title: Deposed by Augustus
events.summary: After complaints from both Jews and Samaritans about his brutality, the emperor Augustus removes him and banishes him to Vienne in Gaul. Judea then comes under direct Roman rule through governors (later including Pontius Pilate).

summary: Archelaus was a son of Herod the Great and a Samaritan wife, Malthace, and full brother of Herod Antipas. When Herod died in 4 BC, Augustus gave Archelaus the central part of the kingdom (Judea, Samaria and Idumea) with the lesser title of ethnarch. His rule was so harsh that in AD 6 Rome removed him and made Judea a Roman province. His date of death is unknown.
textSays: Matthew 2:22 is his only mention by name: Joseph 'heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod' and was afraid.
context: Josephus (*Antiquities* 17.9.3 and 17.13.2) describes him massacring about 3,000 people at the Temple at the start of his reign and his later banishment. When he went to Rome to have his rule confirmed, a delegation of his subjects went after him to protest.

interpretations.view: Many scholars think Jesus' parable of a nobleman who goes to a far country to receive a kingdom while his citizens send a delegation saying 'we do not want this man to reign over us' (Luke 19:12-27) echoes Archelaus's trip to Rome. Others see only a general resemblance to how client kings were appointed.

voice: Insecure and heavy-handed, quick to answer opposition with force.

names.original: Latin Gaius Octavius, later Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus
names.meaning: 'Augustus' means 'revered' or 'majestic', a title given by the Senate in 27 BC

alternatives.label: Sole power after the Battle of Actium

events.title: Becomes sole ruler of the Roman world
events.summary: He defeats Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the naval Battle of Actium, ending Rome's civil wars. In 27 BC the Senate gives him the title Augustus.

events.title: Decree that all the world should be registered
events.summary: Luke says a decree of Augustus for a registration (census) is why Joseph and Mary travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born. The date and nature of this census are debated (see Quirinius).

events.title: Settles Herod's kingdom
events.summary: After Herod the Great's death he divides the kingdom among Herod's sons Archelaus, Antipas and Philip, and in AD 6 removes Archelaus.

summary: Augustus was the first Roman emperor. He ended a century of civil war and ruled from 27 BC to AD 14, a period remembered as the start of the Pax Romana ('Roman peace'). Jesus was born during his reign. Luke names him to set the birth of Jesus on the stage of world history: the most powerful man on earth issues a decree, and it brings a poor couple to Bethlehem.
textSays: Luke 2:1 says a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. He is not named elsewhere in the Bible, though Acts 25:21 uses the title 'Augustus' (Sebastos) for a later emperor.
context: Augustus was honoured in inscriptions as a 'saviour' who brought peace, and the birthday of Augustus was called 'good news' (euangelia) in the Priene calendar inscription of 9 BC. He was officially 'son of the divine' after the deification of Julius Caesar. His own account of his achievements survives as the *Res Gestae Divi Augusti*.

interpretations.view: Many scholars read Luke 2 as a quiet contrast: the angels announce good news, a Saviour, and peace on earth (Luke 2:10-14) using the same vocabulary the empire used for Augustus.

No surviving Roman source mentions a single empire-wide census under Augustus, though he did order many provincial censuses. Some think Luke compresses several of these; others think he refers to a registration in Herod's kingdom (debated).

voice: Calm, cautious and formal, a master of image who speaks of restoring order and the old Roman virtues.

names.original: Latin Tiberius Claudius Nero; as emperor Tiberius Caesar Augustus

roles: Emperor during Jesus' ministry and crucifixion

events.title: Fifteenth year of his reign
events.summary: Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, usually reckoned as AD 28/29 (or AD 26/27 if counted from a shared rule with Augustus).

events.title: 'Render to Caesar'
events.summary: Asked whether paying tax to Caesar is lawful, Jesus asks for a denarius, points to Caesar's image on it, and says to give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's. The coin was most likely a denarius of Tiberius.

events.title: Pilate pressed with his name
events.summary: The crowd warns Pilate, 'If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend,' and the chief priests declare, 'We have no king but Caesar.'

summary: Tiberius was the stepson and adopted heir of Augustus and ruled the Roman Empire from AD 14 to 37. He is the 'Caesar' of the Gospels during Jesus' adult life: Jesus' ministry, crucifixion and resurrection all happened in his reign. The Roman historian Tacitus also dates Jesus' execution under Pontius Pilate to the reign of Tiberius. The city of Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee, built by Herod Antipas, was named after him.
textSays: Luke 3:1 names him directly. The Gospels refer to the reigning emperor simply as 'Caesar' (Matt 22:17-21; Luke 23:2; John 19:12). John 6:23 mentions the city of Tiberias.
context: Tacitus, *Annals* 15.44, says Christ 'suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of the procurator Pontius Pilate' (paraphrased). In his later years Tiberius withdrew to the island of Capri, leaving government largely to the praetorian prefect Sejanus until Sejanus's fall in AD 31.

interpretations.view: Some read Jesus' answer as accepting a legitimate role for government; others stress the second half, that people bear God's image and belong wholly to God, so Caesar's claim is limited. Both readings are widely held.

voice: Gloomy, suspicious and dry; a reluctant ruler who distrusted flattery.

names.original: Latin Publius Sulpicius Quirinius; Greek Kyrēnios

occupations: Roman senator, general and provincial governor

events.title: The census 'when Quirinius was governor of Syria'
events.summary: Luke ties the registration that brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem to the time when Quirinius governed Syria.

events.title: Census of Judea
events.summary: When Judea became a Roman province in AD 6, Quirinius carried out a census for tax purposes. It sparked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean, which Gamaliel mentions in Acts.

summary: Quirinius was a Roman senator and general who served as governor of Syria (which oversaw Judea) and ran a well-known census of Judea in AD 6, according to Josephus. Luke links Jesus' birth to a census under Quirinius. That creates a well-known puzzle, because Matthew and Luke both place Jesus' birth while Herod the Great was alive, and Herod died around 4 BC, about ten years before Quirinius's Judean census.
textSays: Luke 2:2 says 'this was the first registration when Quirinius was governing Syria'. Acts 5:37 mentions the revolt of Judas the Galilean 'in the days of the census'.
context: Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.1.1, describes Quirinius's census of Judea after Archelaus was deposed. Tacitus, *Annals* 3.48, records his death in AD 21.

interpretations.view: Many critical scholars think Luke confused the dates and linked Jesus' birth to the famous AD 6 census.
Some scholars translate Luke 2:2 as 'this registration happened before Quirinius governed Syria', which removes the conflict; critics reply that this is a strained reading of the Greek.

Others argue that Quirinius held an earlier command in the region before 4 BC, or that an earlier census began under Herod and was completed under Quirinius; critics say the evidence for an earlier governorship is thin.

voice: Efficient, ambitious and bureaucratic; he speaks in lists and deadlines.

names.meaning: The text does not give the man's name; 'Legion' is the name the spirits give, after a Roman army unit of about 5,000 soldiers

nation: Decapolis (largely Gentile region east of the Sea of Galilee)
roles: Proclaimer of Jesus in the Decapolis

events.title: Meets Jesus among the tombs
events.summary: Living among the tombs, breaking every chain, crying out and cutting himself, he runs to Jesus. Asked his name, he answers 'Legion, for we are many.'

events.title: The spirits enter the pigs
events.summary: Jesus allows the spirits to enter a herd of about two thousand pigs, which rush into the lake and drown. The townspeople find the man clothed and in his right mind, and in fear they ask Jesus to leave.

events.title: Sent home as a witness
events.summary: He begs to go with Jesus, but Jesus sends him home to tell what the Lord has done. He proclaims it throughout the Decapolis, and everyone marvels.

summary:
This unnamed man lived among the tombs on the eastern, mostly Gentile, side of the Sea of Galilee, tormented by many evil spirits. When Jesus asked his name, the spirits answered 'Legion'. Jesus freed him, and the spirits went into a herd of pigs that rushed into the lake. Instead of letting him join the disciples, Jesus sent him home, and he became the first person to tell Gentile towns about Jesus.

Mark and Luke speak of one man; Matthew speaks of two. The place is given differently in manuscripts and Gospels as the country of the Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes.
textSays: Mark 5:3-5 describes his strength, isolation and self-harm. Mark 5:9 gives the name Legion. Mark 5:15 describes him sitting, clothed and in his right mind. Matthew 8:28 has two men in the country of the Gadarenes.

interpretations.view: Many Christians read the story as a literal deliverance from demonic powers, showing Jesus' authority over evil even in Gentile territory.

Some scholars note the military word 'Legion' and the pigs (the boar was an emblem of a Roman legion stationed in the region) and read the story as also hinting at Roman occupation. Others think this reads too much into it.
Matthew's two men may include a second, less prominent sufferer; Mark and Luke focus on the one who spoke and later preached.

voice: Once wild and broken, now calm, grateful and eager to tell anyone who will listen.

names.meaning: The text does not give his name; a centurion commanded about 80 to 100 Roman soldiers

roles: Roman officer in charge of the crucifixion

events.title: Confession at Jesus' death
events.summary: Seeing how Jesus died, he says, 'Truly this man was the Son of God' (Mark and Matthew), or 'Certainly this man was innocent' (Luke).

events.title: Confirms Jesus' death to Pilate
events.summary: Pilate summons him to confirm that Jesus is already dead before releasing the body to Joseph of Arimathea.

summary: The unnamed centurion supervised Jesus' crucifixion. When Jesus died, he declared him the Son of God (in Mark and Matthew) or innocent (in Luke). In Mark, he is the first human being to call Jesus 'Son of God' after the death on the cross, and he was a Gentile and an executioner.
textSays: Mark 15:39 says he stood facing Jesus and saw how he breathed his last. Matthew 27:54 says he and those with him saw the earthquake and were terrified. Luke 23:47 says he praised God. Mark 15:44-45 has him report Jesus' death to Pilate.

interpretations.view: Many see his words as a full confession of faith that forms the climax of Mark's Gospel (compare Mark 1:1).

The Greek can also be read 'a son of God', which a pagan soldier might have meant in a more limited sense; scholars debate how much he understood, though Mark clearly intends readers to hear the full meaning.

traditions.text: Later tradition named him Longinus and often merged him with the unnamed soldier who pierced Jesus' side with a spear (John 19:34). Tradition says he became a Christian and a martyr. The Gospels give no name.
traditions.source: Acts of Pilate (Gospel of Nicodemus), later recensions; Western martyrologies

voice: Hardened and matter-of-fact, then suddenly awed, speaking with a soldier's bluntness.

names.meaning: 'Joined' or 'attached'

events.title: Called from the tax booth; hosts a feast
events.summary: Jesus sees Levi at his tax booth and says 'Follow me'; he leaves everything and follows. He then holds a great feast for Jesus with many tax collectors and sinners, and Jesus answers critics: 'I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.'

summary: Levi is the name Mark and Luke give to the tax collector whom Jesus called from his booth at Capernaum. Matthew's Gospel tells the same story but calls the man Matthew, and lists 'Matthew the tax collector' among the Twelve. So most readers, ancient and modern, take Levi and Matthew to be one person with two names. This is a short cross-reference profile; see Matthew for the full story.
textSays: Mark 2:14 calls him 'Levi the son of Alphaeus'. Luke 5:27-29 calls him Levi and says he made a great feast. Matthew 9:9 tells the same call of 'a man named Matthew', and Matthew 10:3 lists 'Matthew the tax collector' among the apostles. No list of the Twelve includes a Levi.

interpretations.view: Most identify Levi with Matthew: the stories are nearly identical, and Jews of the time often had two names (compare Simon/Peter, Saul/Paul). 'Matthew' may have been a new name given by Jesus or a second name.

A few, ancient and modern, distinguish them. Clement of Alexandria quotes the second-century teacher Heracleon listing Matthew and Levi separately. Some modern scholars think Matthew's Gospel deliberately put the apostle's name into Mark's story.
Because Levi is 'son of Alphaeus' and an apostle is 'James son of Alphaeus' (Mark 3:18), some suggest they were brothers; Alphaeus was a common name and the Gospels never say so.

voice: Shrewd with money and used to scorn, now generous and glad to throw open his house.

names.meaning: 'God has given'

events.title: 'Can anything good come out of Nazareth?'
events.summary: Philip tells him they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael scoffs, but comes. Jesus calls him 'an Israelite in whom there is no deceit' and says he saw him under the fig tree. Nathanael confesses, 'You are the Son of God, the King of Israel,' and Jesus promises he will see greater things.

events.title: At the lakeside appearance of the risen Jesus
events.summary: He is among the seven disciples fishing on the Sea of Galilee when the risen Jesus appears and provides a large catch.

summary: Nathanael appears only in John's Gospel, as one of the first people Jesus called and later as one of the disciples who saw the risen Jesus by the Sea of Galilee. John says he came from Cana. He is traditionally identified with Bartholomew, one of the Twelve, but the Bible never makes that link directly. This is a short cross-reference profile; see Bartholomew for the apostle's wider story.
textSays: John 1:45-49 tells his call and confession. John 21:2 calls him 'Nathanael of Cana in Galilee'. He does not appear in the lists of the Twelve, which name Bartholomew instead (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13).

interpretations.view: In the first three Gospels Bartholomew is listed right after Philip, and in John it is Philip who brings Nathanael. 'Bartholomew' is a family name meaning 'son of Tolmai', so the man may also have had a personal name, Nathanael. John never mentions Bartholomew, and the other Gospels never mention Nathanael. This identification became common in the medieval church.

interpretations.tradition: Not one of the Twelve (minority view)
interpretations.view: Some, including Augustine in his sermons on John, thought Nathanael was not one of the Twelve at all; John uses the word 'disciples' more broadly than 'the Twelve'.

voice: Frank and a little skeptical, with a dry wit, but quick to give his whole heart once convinced.

names.primary: Lazarus (in the parable of the rich man)
names.meaning: 'God has helped'

events.title: The rich man and Lazarus
events.summary: A poor man covered with sores lies at a rich man's gate, longing for scraps, while dogs lick his sores. Both die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side; the rich man is in torment in Hades. Abraham says a great gulf is fixed between them and refuses to send Lazarus to warn the rich man's brothers, because 'if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.'

summary: Lazarus is the poor beggar in a story Jesus told in Luke 16. He is the only character in any of Jesus' parables who is given a personal name. His name means 'God has helped', fitting a man helped by no one on earth. He is a different person from Lazarus of Bethany, whom Jesus raised from the dead in John 11.
textSays: Luke 16:20-21 describes him lying at the gate, covered with sores. Luke 16:22 says he died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side ('bosom'). Luke 16:25 contrasts what each man received in life. He never speaks in the story.

interpretations.view: Most interpreters read it as a parable teaching about wealth, compassion and the sufficiency of Scripture. Some, noting the personal name and the absence of 'a parable' label, argue Jesus was describing real people.

interpretations.tradition: What it teaches about the afterlife (debated)
interpretations.view: Some take its picture of Hades and 'Abraham's bosom' as real information about the state after death; others think Jesus used familiar Jewish imagery to make a moral point, so details should not be pressed. See /afterlife.

Some readers note the ending, about someone rising from the dead and still not being believed, and connect it with the raising of Lazarus in John 11, after which leaders plotted against Jesus. This link is suggestive but not stated.

traditions.text: Medieval tradition called the rich man 'Dives' (Latin for 'rich man'), and Lazarus became the patron of lepers; hospitals for lepers were called 'lazar houses'.
traditions.source: Latin Vulgate wording of Luke 16:19; medieval European usage

voice: Silent in the story; if he spoke, he would speak softly, without bitterness, as one who has finally been comforted.

names.meaning: The text does not give his name; the title combines details from three Gospels

roles: Wealthy seeker who declined Jesus' call
occupations: Man of great wealth; a 'ruler' (possibly a synagogue or local leader)

events.title: 'What must I do to inherit eternal life?'
events.summary: He runs up, kneels, and asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. He says he has kept the commandments since his youth. Jesus, looking at him, loves him, and tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow. He goes away sorrowful, for he has great possessions.

summary: This unnamed man came to Jesus asking how to gain eternal life. He had kept the commandments, and Mark says Jesus looked at him and loved him. But when Jesus told him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow him, he went away sad. The common name 'rich young ruler' combines details: all three Gospels say he was rich, only Matthew says he was young, and only Luke calls him a ruler.
textSays: Mark 10:21 says Jesus loved him. Matthew 19:20 calls him a young man; Luke 18:18 calls him a ruler. All three record Jesus' saying that it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:25).

interpretations.view: Some Christians (for example many in the monastic and Anabaptist traditions) see the command to sell everything as a real call to voluntary poverty for those who would follow Jesus fully.
Others read it as a command aimed at this man's particular attachment to wealth, showing that whatever rules a person's heart must be surrendered, rather than a rule for every believer.

Some Protestant readers see Jesus exposing the limits of law-keeping, since the man could not do the one thing asked; the disciples' question 'Who then can be saved?' is answered: 'with God all things are possible' (Mark 10:27).

voice: Earnest, polite and sincere, used to doing things right, and visibly torn.

names.primary: The widow of Nain and her son
names.meaning: The text names neither mother nor son
aliases: Son of the widow of Nain

roles: Young man raised from the dead

events.title: Raised at the town gate
events.summary: Jesus meets a funeral procession for the only son of a widow. Moved with compassion, he tells her 'Do not weep', touches the bier, and says 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' The dead man sits up and begins to speak, and Jesus gives him back to his mother. The crowd says, 'A great prophet has arisen among us; God has visited his people.'

summary: At the gate of the village of Nain in Galilee, Jesus met the funeral of a young man, the only son of a widow. Without being asked, he raised him to life and 'gave him to his mother'. Luke alone tells the story. For a widow in that society, losing her only son could mean losing her means of support, so the miracle restored both of them.
textSays: Luke 7:12 says he was 'the only son of his mother, and she was a widow'. Luke 7:13 says the Lord had compassion on her. Luke 7:15 says Jesus gave him to his mother, words that echo Elijah raising the widow of Zarephath's son (1 Kgs 17:23).

interpretations.view: Most commentators note the parallel with Elijah (1 Kgs 17:17-24) and Elisha, who raised the Shunammite's son at nearby Shunem (2 Kgs 4:32-37). The crowd's cry that a great prophet has arisen shows they understood the link.
The story is often used to show Jesus' compassion for the grieving and for vulnerable women, since he acts before anyone asks.

voice: The mother: numb with grief, then overwhelmed. The son: confused, then joyfully talking.

names.meaning: The text does not give her name; 'Syrophoenician' means a Phoenician from the province of Syria

roles: Gentile mother who sought healing for her daughter

events.title: 'Even the dogs eat the children's crumbs'
events.summary: In the region of Tyre she begs Jesus to free her daughter from an unclean spirit. Jesus answers that the children (Israel) must be fed first and it is not right to throw their bread to the dogs. She replies that even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs. Jesus praises her answer (in Matthew, her great faith) and her daughter is healed at a distance.

summary: This unnamed Gentile woman came to Jesus near Tyre to ask him to heal her daughter. Jesus' first reply sounds harsh, using a common image of Gentiles as 'dogs'. She did not argue against him but took his own words and turned them into a request, and he granted it. She is the only person in the Gospels who wins an exchange of words with Jesus.
textSays: Mark 7:26 calls her 'a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth'. Matthew 15:22 calls her 'a Canaanite woman' and has her address Jesus as 'Son of David'. Matthew 15:24 has Jesus say he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel. Matthew 15:28 has Jesus say 'great is your faith'.

interpretations.view: Many traditional interpreters say Jesus was testing and drawing out her faith, knowing he would help her.
Others stress that Jesus' mission was to Israel first, then to the nations (compare Rom 1:16), and that her story anticipates the Gentile mission.

Some modern interpreters think Jesus, being truly human, was genuinely moved by her reply to widen the scope of his ministry; others object that this conflicts with his knowledge and purpose elsewhere.

traditions.text: The Pseudo-Clementine writings name her Justa and her daughter Bernice.

voice: Desperate but clever, humble but unwilling to take no for an answer.

names.meaning: The text does not give her name

events.title: 'Let him who is without sin cast the first stone'
events.summary: In the Temple courts, scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery and ask whether she should be stoned as the Law of Moses commands, hoping to trap Jesus. He writes on the ground, then says that whoever is without sin should throw the first stone. They leave one by one. Jesus tells her, 'Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.'

summary: This unnamed woman was brought to Jesus in the Temple as a test case: should she be stoned for adultery? Jesus turned the question back on her accusers, who left, and then sent her away uncondemned but told to stop sinning. The story is one of the best loved in the Gospels, but it is also the best known textual puzzle in the New Testament: it is missing from the earliest and most important manuscripts of John.
textSays: John 8:4-5 records the charge and the appeal to the Law (compare Lev 20:10; Deut 22:22). John 8:6 says they were testing him. John 8:7 records his saying about the first stone. John 8:11 records his words to her. The man involved is not mentioned.
context: The passage (John 7:53-8:11) does not appear in the earliest Greek manuscripts of John (including Papyrus 66, Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus). It first appears in a Greek manuscript in Codex Bezae (about AD 400), and in other manuscripts it is placed elsewhere, for example after Luke 21:38 or after John 7:36. Modern Bibles usually print it with a note or in brackets.

interpretations.tradition: Not original to John, but authentic tradition (scholarly consensus on the first part)
interpretations.view: Most textual scholars agree it was not part of John as first written. Many still think it preserves a genuine early story about Jesus, which circulated separately before being added to John.
A minority argue it was originally in John and was removed early, perhaps because some feared it seemed too lenient on adultery.
Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches treat it as Scripture or as a reliable account, while being open about its textual history.

voice: Terrified and silent at first, then stunned to be spoken to with dignity.

names.meaning: The text does not give his name; a centurion commanded about 80 to 100 soldiers

nation: Gentile soldier, probably in Herod Antipas's service
roles: Gentile officer whose servant Jesus healed

gifts.name: Faith that Jesus' word is enough

events.title: 'Only say the word'
events.summary: His valued servant is paralysed and near death. He asks Jesus for help but says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof: as a man under authority who gives orders, he knows Jesus need only speak. Jesus marvels and says he has not found such faith in Israel. The servant is healed at that hour.

summary: This unnamed centurion was a Gentile officer stationed at Capernaum, probably serving Herod Antipas rather than the Roman army directly. He loved the Jewish people and had built their synagogue. When his servant was dying, he trusted that Jesus could heal from a distance by a word, and Jesus said he had not found such faith anywhere in Israel. His words 'Lord, I am not worthy' are still repeated in many communion liturgies.
textSays: Matthew 8:5-6 has the centurion come to Jesus himself. Luke 7:3-6 has him send Jewish elders and then friends, who say he loves the nation and built the synagogue. Matthew 8:11-12 adds Jesus' saying that many will come from east and west to sit with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

interpretations.view: Ancient custom treated a messenger as the sender, so Matthew may simply shorten the story by having the centurion speak directly, while Luke gives the fuller account.
Some scholars think John's story of a royal official at Capernaum whose son is healed from Cana (John 4:46-54) is a version of the same event; others think it is a separate miracle.
Catholic, Anglican and other liturgies adapt his words before communion: 'Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word.'

voice: Disciplined, respectful and economical with words, a commander who knows the power of a single order.
